transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2028-09-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 min | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Noah Patel (Redwood Product), Priya Nair (Monsoon Head of ML), Ethan Cole (Platform), Sara Ahmed (Security), Jordan Lee (PM)

Summary: Quick demo showing schema stewardship in the console, how to bind schemas to model outputs, and runtime action flows that safely call internal tools (e.g., payment lookup, trade enrichment). Walked through fallback policies, canary routing, and a proposed dedicated pilot for latency-sensitive fraud scoring.

[00:00] Maya Chen: All right everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have, uh, 45, 50 minutes scheduled, we'll aim for demo first, then Q&A. Priya, want to do a 30 second intro?
[00:10] Priya Nair: Yeah sure. I'm Priya, head of ML at Monsoon. We're trying to standardize outputs from models across trading and risk products, and want safer tool integration for enrichment calls. Latency under 120ms is tough for some of our endpoints.
[00:25] Luis Ortega: Great context, thanks. Quick note — when I say JSON mode I'm referring to Redwood's typed response mode where you pin a schema and the runtime validates and can auto-correct. It's also how you enable safe tool invocation.
[00:38] Ethan Cole: Sorry quick Q — does that add heh a lot of overhead to latency? If we validate schemas at runtime won't that be slowing tokens or whatever.
[00:50] Luis Ortega: Good question. The validation is lightweight; the biggest impact is if you use synchronous tool calls or wait for external enrichment. We demo two patterns today: in-line schema enforcement with auto-repair and async tool fan-out with cached results to keep p99s low.
[01:12] Jordan Lee: Also curious about how we manage evolution of schemas — our contracts change a lot, we don't want to break production.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Perfect, we'll show the console's schema registry and rollout controls, plus the automatic evals and regression alerts in Redwood Optimize.

[01:35] Demo start - Console:
[01:37] Luis Ortega: Here is the console - I'm opening the "Schema Steward" page. You can see a list of response contracts, version history. I'm uploading a sample schema for trade-enrichment response — fields: trade_id, seller, buyer, risk_score, enrichment_metadata. Note, the demo data is synthetic.
[02:05] Priya Nair: The UI looks neat. How do you handle unknown fields?
[02:12] Luis Ortega: Two options: strict (reject) or permissive (strip unknowns and surface warnings). Many teams pick permissive for a gradual rollout. We also have a canary rule so 10% of traffic uses the new schema until you're happy.
[02:30] Ethan Cole: And the canary can be pinned to region? we have eu-west-1 constraints for some data residency.
[02:38] Luis Ortega: Yep, routing policies include region, tier, and model variant. You can route eu traffic to VPC/private infra too.

[03:05] Luis Ortega: Next: function calls. I'm wiring up a tool that hits Monsoon's internal enrichment API — note in the console you define the tool signature and which fields are passed. We enforce parameter typing and we can mask sensitive inputs.
[03:30] Sara Ahmed: Masking sounds good — can we restrict logs for those calls? We need audit trails but not plain-text keys in logs.
[03:40] Noah Patel: On the security side, Redwood supports KMS-backed key management and you can opt to redact sensitive params from traces. Audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM and retention is configurable per tenant.
[03:55] Sara Ahmed: Do you provide SOC 2 docs? Also we use a hardware HSM..
[04:00] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send the SOC 2 package. HSM integration via customer-managed KMS is supported for Private deployments. I'll add that to the action items.

[04:20] Live coding: schema + tool flow
[04:22] Luis Ortega: I'm going to test the flow — prompt: "Enrich trade 98765, return schema." The model suggests an enrichment with a nested metadata object — Redwood's runtime validates and we see two things: the response matches schema, or we get a repair suggestion.
[04:45] Priya Nair: Wait, repair suggestion? How reliable is that? We can't have random guesses ant the model rewriting risk scores.
[04:55] Luis Ortega: The repair is conservative: it only fills missing fields with deterministic defaults or fails the call depending on policy. You can set auto-repair off for critical fields like risk_score.
[05:10] Ethan Cole: Ok that helps. For the enrichment tool, can we make calls idempotent? we don't want duplicate billing or writes.
[05:20] Luis Ortega: The tool definition can include a call_id param and Redwood will dedupe at the runtime layer if you enable idempotency.

[05:35] [06:00] Break / background noise — muffled conversation (office)
[06:20] Jordan Lee: Back to rollouts — how do you detect regressions?
[06:30] Noah Patel: Optimize hooks let you tie an eval suite to a schema version — you run blind holdout sets and get alerts if quality drops beyond thresholds. You can also monitor token-level cost and per-route latency.
[06:50] Priya Nair: We have a sensitive eval set for fraud; can we run Redwood's evals on premise?
[07:00] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we can run evals in your VPC, yes. We also offer data residency options.

[07:15] Deep-dive: Runtime fallbacks
[07:20] Luis Ortega: Consider a runtime policy: primary model (quantized, low-cost) -> if hallucination risk high or schema mismatch -> fallback to higher-precision model or call enrichment tool -> if enrichment fails -> fallback to cached value or safe default. The policies are configurable and you can set SLOs per route.
[07:50] Priya Nair: How do you measure hallucination risk?
[07:55] Luis Ortega: A few signals: model calibration score, schema mismatch delta, and prompt-level safety checks. We offer a composite confidence metric you can threshold.

[08:20] Sara Ahmed: For audit we need to preserve original model outputs for forensics but hide tokens with PII. Is that supported?
[08:30] Noah Patel: Yes, redact on ingest, store masked transcripts, and maintain verifiable hashes for audit. We can also stream logs to your audit cluster.

[08:50] [09:05] Question from Ethan: If we do dedicated GPUs, how does autoscaling work?
[09:12] Luis Ortega: Dedicated pools support configurable autoscaling and burst policies. For low-latency endpoints you can reserve headrooms and set failover to hosted or another region.
[09:28] Priya Nair: Cost — any ballpark for a pilot that hits ~100k inference calls per day with p50 ~80ms?
[09:40] Maya Chen: We'll run a quick estimate post-call. Roughly depends on batching config, sequence length, and quantization. Luis can propose a mix — dedciated for hot endpoints + hosted for long tail.

[10:05] Live scenario: Fraud-scoring flow
[10:10] Luis Ortega: I'm going to simulate a fraud scoring request. Notice the prompt includes a call to the customer tool 'account_lookup' and 'tx_hist' which return JSON. Redwood's runtime enforces the tool schema and will reject unexpected fields or values.
[10:35] Priya Nair: If a tool returns malformed JSON, will that break the chain?
[10:40] Luis Ortega: We have sanitizer adapters — you can add a transformer to normalize tool outputs, or set fallback to cached snapshot.

[11:00] Interruptions / chatty aside: someone mentions "KV cash" (kv cache) and there's a little laugh.
[11:10] Maya Chen: That was fine, but worth noting KV cache improves latency for repeated prompts with similar prefixes. For trade enrichment it can save a lot of cost.

[11:30] Security specifics
[11:32] Sara Ahmed: A few musts: SSO/SAML + RBAC, per-route audit logs, key management with customer kms, and ability to run private control plane.
[11:45] Maya Chen: All supported — Private gives you control plane in your VPC, HSM/KMS integrations are supported, and RBAC maps to SSO groups. We'll include mapping examples in the security packet.

[12:00] Question: Data retention and deletion requirements
[12:05] Noah Patel: Retention is configurable. For Private you can set zero retention for request payloads and only keep metrics. For Hosted we offer per-account retention controls and delete-on-demand APIs.

[12:40] Pricing and pilots
[12:45] Maya Chen: For pilots, we typically propose a time-boxed dedicated pool with a usage commit. That gives you predictable latency and isolation. We'll propose cost and a plan to move to reserved commit if it proves out.
[13:10] Ethan Cole: Any prep we should do before the benchmark?
[13:15] Luis Ortega: Provide representative prompt shapes, average sequence length, and regional constraints. Also share a small eval set we can run.

[13:35] Q&A rapid fire:
[13:38] Priya Nair: Can Redwood call internal DBs behind our firewall?
[13:42] Maya Chen: Yes via private deployment or VPC peering with the private control plane.
[13:48] Jordan Lee: How do we monitor cost attribution?
[13:52] Noah Patel: Console shows per-route and per-token breakdowns, plus per-token cost by model variant and batching efficiency.

[14:05] Closing demo bits: Canary example
[14:10] Luis Ortega: I'll create a canary rule: 5% traffic routes to new schema+model. If error rate or regression > threshold, auto-roll back.
[14:30] Priya Nair: Love auto-rollback. Saves a lot of stress.

[14:40] Final recap
[14:42] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll send: pilot SOW & pricing, SOC2/KMS docs, sample schema repo, and proposed pilot config. Action items in the notes. Next meeting: benchmark deep-dive week of 2028-09-18.
[14:58] Sara Ahmed: Thanks, please cc security on the docs.
[15:03] Priya Nair: Thanks, great session.
[15:05] Meeting ends

Notes on transcription: There are occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache), and a few timestamps approximate. Speaker labels are a mix of names and roles as captured by the recorder. Some proprietary internal tool names were redacted by request during the call.
